slides.text: Generative adversarial networks (GAN) consist of a generator and a discriminator that compete over the true data distribution $p_\text{data}$ and the model distribution $p_g$.
At the start of training, the generator is bad and the discriminator is untrained.
Training alternates: first the discriminator is trained a little, then the generator improves to catch up.
The generator and discriminator keep alternating training until both converge.
The generator is a function $G = G(z; \theta_g) : Z \to X$.
The discriminator is a function $D = D(x; \theta_d) : X \to [0, 1]$.
The discriminator solves a binary classification problem with the loss $\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{data}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g(x)}[\log(1 - D(x))]$.
Training uses two mini-batches: one with labels $0$ from the generator and one with labels $1$ from the real data.
The generator minimizes $\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]$.
The GAN training is a minimax game: $\min_G \max_D V(D, G)$ with $V(D, G) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{data}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]$.
For a fixed generator $G$, the optimal discriminator is $D^*_G(x) = \frac{p_\text{data}(x)}{p_\text{data}(x) + p_g(x)}$.
The global minimum of the minimax criterion is achieved if and only if $p_g = p_\text{data}$.

At the optimal discriminator, the minimax criterion equals the Jensen–Shannon divergence between $p_\text{data}$ and $p_g$: $\operatorname{KL}\left(p_\text{data} \Big\| \frac{p_\text{data} + p_g}{2}\right) + \operatorname{KL}\left(p_g \Big\| \frac{p_\text{data} + p_g}{2}\right)$.
In a classifier, cross-entropy does not saturate when the answer is wrong, and saturates when the answer is right.
When the discriminator performs well, the gradient from minimizing $\log(1 - D(G(z)))$ vanishes, causing the generator gradient to also vanish.
In practice, the generator minimizes $-\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log D(G(z))]$ to maximize the probability that the discriminator makes a mistake.
In the training algorithm, with fixed generator, the discriminator is updated to maximize $\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{data}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g(x)}[\log(1 - D(x))]$.
With fixed discriminator, the generator is updated to minimize $-\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log D(G(z))]$.
DCGAN uses strided convolutions instead of pooling.
DCGAN uses batch normalisation throughout.
DCGAN removes fully connected layers.
DCGAN uses the Adam optimiser.
On LSUN bedrooms, after one epoch, DCGAN generates coarse room structures.
After five epochs, DCGAN generates much sharper, realistic bedrooms.
Walking through the feature space of a DCGAN produces smooth transitions in generated images.
Removing filters that detect windows from a DCGAN removes windows from generated images.
Vector arithmetic in the latent space of a DCGAN, like in word2vec, allows operations such as 'man with glasses' minus 'man' plus 'woman' yields 'woman with glasses'.
DCGAN can be applied to generate pixel art from NES games.
GANs have problems with counting objects.
GANs have problems with perspective.
ProGAN trains the GAN to generate images at increasing resolutions, starting from $4 \times 4$, doubling each stage.
ProGAN gradually increases resolution up to $1024 \times 1024$.
In ProGAN, new layers are added progressively, and the discriminator remains roughly symmetric to the generator.
ProGAN saves training time because it can show more data per wall-clock time.
For some categories, ProGAN stops resolution at $256 \times 256$, which already yields very good images.
Least Squares GAN (LSGAN) addresses the saturation problem of Jensen–Shannon divergence when $p_g$ is far from $p_\text{data}$.
Standard GAN discriminators use a logistic sigmoid, which can lead to vanishing gradients.
In LSGAN, the discriminator loss is $\frac12 \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{data}}[(D(x) - b)^2] + \frac12 \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[(D(G(z)) - a)^2]$.
In LSGAN, the generator loss is $\frac12 \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[(D(G(z)) - c)^2]$.
The discriminator learns to output $a$ for fake data and $b$ for real data; the generator wants it to output $c$ for fakes.
Typically $a = 0$, $b = 1$, $c = 1$.
LSGAN is more robust to architectural changes, suffers less from mode collapse, and its quadratic loss is widely used.
InfoGAN adds disentanglement to GANs so that different latent dimensions correspond to meaningful features.
InfoGAN splits the input into noise $z$ and a latent code $c$.
InfoGAN maximizes the mutual information $I(c, G(z, c))$ to prevent the generator from ignoring the latent code $c$.
InfoGAN uses a variational lower bound on mutual information, parameterized by a network $Q$ similar to $D$.
On MNIST, InfoGAN uses $c_1$ as a discrete label with $10$ categories (uniform prior, unsupervised), and $c_2, c_3$ uniform continuous factors.
Using only the code $c_1$, a classifier on MNIST generated by InfoGAN achieves $5\%$ error without labels.
InfoGAN has been applied to generate 3D faces and 3D chairs.
Minimizing KL divergence requires the model distribution to exist everywhere, otherwise it can be infinite if supports do not overlap.
Adding noise to make KL divergence well-defined results in blurry generated samples.
A distance metric that is well-behaved on low-dimensional supports is needed for generative models.

The Earth Mover (Wasserstein-1) distance is defined as $W(p_\text{data}, p_\text{model}) = \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(p_\text{data}, p_\text{model})} \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim \gamma}[\|x - y\|]$, where $\Pi$ is the set of joint distributions with marginals $p_\text{data}$ and $p_\text{model}$.
In a simple example with shifting line distributions, only the Earth Mover distance converges continuously as parameters approach zero, while other distances diverge.
The continuous behavior of the Earth Mover distance is crucial for learning distributions on submanifolds.

By Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality, the Earth Mover distance equals $\sup_{\|f\|_L \le 1} \left(\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{data}}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{model}}[f(x)]\right)$, where the supremum is over $1$-Lipschitz functions.
WGAN uses a critic $f_w$ parameterized by a neural network, instead of a discriminator.
In WGAN training, for fixed generator, the critic is trained to maximize $\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{data}}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{model}}[f(x)]$.
The generator gradient in WGAN, with fixed critic, is $-\mathbb{E}_{z \sim Z}[\nabla_\theta f_w(g_\theta(z))]$.
WGAN enforces the Lipschitz constraint by weight clipping.
WGAN allows the critic to be trained to convergence, unlike the ordinary GAN discriminator.
The WGAN loss value strongly correlates with sample quality.
WGAN is robust to architectural changes, still producing reasonable results without batchnorm or with fewer filters.
Improved WGAN (WGAN-GP) addresses weight clipping issues by using a gradient penalty: $\lambda \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x} \sim \mathbb{P}_{\hat{x}}}[(\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1)^2]$.
Self-Attention GAN (SAGAN) addresses the locality limitation of convolutional generators.
SAGAN applies self-attention, adapted from the Transformer, to images.
SAGAN's generator can attend to distant regions, as confirmed by attention map visualizations.
SAGAN produces good results.
BigGAN improved the Inception score threefold over SAGAN by adding architectural tricks.
The Inception Score uses the Inception classifier to obtain $p(y \mid x)$ for generated images.
A good generator according to Inception Score has low-entropy conditional labels $p(y \mid x)$ and high-entropy marginal label distribution $p(y)$.
The Inception Score is defined as $\exp(\mathbb{E}_x \operatorname{KL}(p(y \mid x) \| p(y)))$.
The Inception Score is difficult to use for training but works well for evaluation.
Adversarial Autoencoders (AAE) use a discriminator to match the encoder's hidden feature distribution to a prior $p(z)$.
Making AAE conditional enables semi-supervised learning.
AAE has been applied to generating molecules in oncology.
druGAN is a molecule generation model that uses adversarial training and compares with VAE.
MOSES is a platform for comparing generative models for molecules.
Conditional GANs (cGAN) receive a condition vector along with the random noise as input to the generator.
Conditional GANs have been used for face aging.
ESRGAN is a conditional GAN for super-resolution.
Stacked GANs (SGAN) chain several GANs sequentially.
In SGAN, each generator $G_i$ learns to invert a deep encoder $E_i$ to generate lower-level representations.
SGAN uses a conditional loss to ensure the generator uses the condition: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{cond}} = \mathbb{E}[d(E_i(G_i(h_{i+1}, z_i)), h_{i+1})]$.
SGAN uses an entropy loss to prevent the generator from ignoring noise: $\mathcal{L}_{\text{ent}} = \mathbb{E}[-\log Q_i(z_i \mid \hat{h}_i)]$, a variational bound on conditional entropy.
SGAN outperforms prior stacked GANs, but ProGAN outperforms SGAN.

transcript.text: The lecture discusses generative adversarial networks (GANs).
GANs are an idea that is initially non-mathematical but logically compelling and leads to elegant mathematics later.
"Generative AI" is not a precisely defined term.
Even logistic regression generates a probability distribution over classes.
The key divide in generative AI is that generative models produce something big—an object of high dimension and complicated structure, such as an image or text.
Deep generative models write, draw, produce music or videos.
The lecture focuses on deep generative models based on neural networks.
The first major fork in deep generative models is between explicit density models and implicit density models.
In a generative model, the output $x$ lives in a very high-dimensional space with an extremely complicated distribution $p(x)$.
In an explicit density model, the model provides an explicit formula for $p(x)$ (or at least an approximation), enabling evaluation in principle.
In an implicit density model, there is no formula for $p(x)$; the model simply samples from the distribution.
Inside explicit density models, the next divide is tractable density models.
Tractable density models allow actually writing down a formula for $p(x)$.
The classic approach in tractable density models is autoregressive modeling, which uses the chain rule: $p(x) = p(x_1) p(x_2 \mid x_1) p(x_3 \mid x_1, x_2) \dots p(x_n \mid x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})$.
The chain rule identity is always true but useless in practice because the conditionals are still huge.

One simplifies autoregressive modeling by making assumptions, such as a Markov assumption where each $x_k$ depends only on a few previous variables, or using an RNN where each output depends on the current input and a hidden state.
Most LLMs are in the autoregressive class, modeling text by predicting the next token $p(x_k \mid \text{context})$ with transformers modeling the conditionals.
For images, PixelCNN once generated pixels one by one, producing good outputs but being far too slow because generating a million pixels requires a million model runs.
Pixel-wise autoregressive models are rarely used today, though they exist.
For text, essentially everything is autoregressive.
Within tractable density models, flow-based models also exist.

Flow-based models model $p(x)$ as a composition of simple transformations: $x = f_k \circ f_{k-1} \circ \dots \circ f_1(z)$, where each $f_i$ is something like adding Gaussian noise or a linear transformation.
Composing many simple transformations can model very complex distributions, just as with deep neural networks.
Explicit density models also include approximate density models, apart from tractable density.
In approximate density models, $p(x)$ is explicitly approximated by a simpler distribution $q$, for example, a product of easier factors.
The most important example of approximate density models is the variational autoencoder (VAE).
VAEs use variational approximations to derive good loss functions for generative models.
VAEs are used extensively.
Diffusion models, the topic of the next lecture, typically operate in the latent space of a VAE.
The implicit density side is much less rich; there are very few mainstream examples.
The primary example of an implicit density model is GANs.
In an implicit density model, there is no formula for $p(x)$ at all.
Implicit density models take random noise (e.g., a standard Gaussian) and transform it into a sample drawn from the target distribution; they are samplers, not explicit distributions.
The neural network in an implicit density model is a black box mapping a simple distribution to a complicated one; a density formula cannot be extracted.
GANs do precisely this: take random noise and transform it into samples.
GANs are one possible solution to the problem of finding a loss function for generative models.
The main problem when creating a generative model is finding the loss function to score the results.
In GANs, the generator takes random noise $Z$ from a standard distribution and maps it to an output $\hat{X}$ intended to be a cat picture.
In this setting, there is a dataset of real images $X$, but no paired data exists between random noise $Z$ and specific real images.
The goal of learning a generator is to learn the mapping from noise to images and to obtain a good parameterization in noise space so that sampling random noise yields reasonable cat pictures.
The data is unlabeled; it is unsupervised learning.
We cannot say which specific $X$ a generated $\hat{X}$ should be similar to; we only desire that $\hat{X}$ is a good cat picture.
There is no mathematical function to determine whether a set of pixels is a good cat picture; learning such a function is half or more of the problem.
GANs recognize that the loss function must be learned because there is no fixed formula for evaluating how cat-like an image looks.
GANs introduce a separate network, the discriminator, whose only job is to classify inputs as fake (0) or real (1).
The discriminator receives an image; if it is from the generator, it should output 0; if it is from the dataset, it should output 1.
The generator and discriminator are adversarial: the discriminator learns to distinguish real from generated images, and the generator learns to fool the discriminator.
This adversarial setup is called adversarial training.
For the last few years, GANs have not been at the forefront of image generation; diffusion models generate images these days.
Adversarial training is still very much alive.
Even in diffusion models, a GAN is embedded to improve them.
Adversarial training is a very important idea in machine learning and appears in many different fields.
The main idea of GANs is that the generator is like a forger producing counterfeit pictures, and the discriminator is the detective deciding whether a picture is real.
The generator, such as a reverse deep convolutional neural network, learns to produce pictures of money.
Initially, the generator produces random noise or very bad counterfeits.
An initially untrained discriminator might be fooled by these early counterfeits.
After training the discriminator, it learns to distinguish the counterfeits as not real money.
Then the generator is trained to fool this current version of the discriminator, producing slightly better counterfeits.
The discriminator finds new features to discriminate on, and the generator learns to fake those features.
This adversarial process continues in a game-like fashion, with the hope of reaching an idealized outcome.
In the idealized picture, in $Z$ space there is a uniform distribution, and in $X$ space there is a Gaussian distribution (green); the black dots are the data points.
Initially, the Gaussian does not match the data points.
The discriminator is a logistic sigmoid (blue dashed line) distinguishing real from fake.
The generator moves the Gaussian slightly to fool the discriminator, without perfectly matching the data.
The discriminator then adapts, and the cycle repeats.
Ideally, the process reaches a state where the generator produces perfect samples and the discriminator cannot distinguish and outputs a coin flip.
In real life, the training does not work exactly like this idealized picture.
The discriminator loss $L_D$ is defined such that the discriminator outputs 0 for fake and 1 for real.
For a real sample $x$, the discriminator's loss includes $\log D(x)$ to push the score to positive infinity, making the probability approach 1.
For a real sample $x$, the discriminator’s loss is $-\log D(x)$.
For a fake sample $x$ from the generator distribution $p_g(x)$, the discriminator’s loss is $-\log(1-D(x))$.
Minimizing this loss with respect to the discriminator’s parameters while the generator is fixed is a straightforward binary classification problem.
The generator aims to produce samples that the discriminator classifies as real.
The generator cannot affect the loss on real data; for the fake data term, it does the opposite of the discriminator.
The generator minimizes $-\log D(G(z))$ (or equivalently $+\log(1-D(G(z)))$) for fake samples.

The adversarial game can be expressed with a shared loss function $V(D,G)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\text{data}}}[\log D(x)]+\mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_z}[\log(1-D(G(z)))]$, where the discriminator maximizes it and the generator minimizes it.
This setup is a minimax problem from game theory.
The minimax problem is notoriously hard.
If the generator is fixed, the optimal discriminator is the Bayes classifier: $p(\text{real}|x) = \frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_{\text{data}}(x)+p_g(x)}$.
Plugging this optimal discriminator into the generator’s objective shows that the generator attains its global minimum if and only if $p_g = p_{\text{data}}$.
Under the optimal discriminator, the generator minimizes the Jensen–Shannon divergence between $p_g$ and $p_{\text{data}}$, not the KL divergence.
These theoretical results are ultimately irrelevant in practice.
In practice, using the flipped binary cross-entropy as the generator loss saturates, which is a bad idea.
The discriminator's output goes through a sigmoid; when the discriminator is very confident and correct, its gradients become extremely small.
For the discriminator, vanishing gradients are harmless, but for the generator, they are catastrophic because the backpropagation signal to the generator must travel through the discriminator.
Once the discriminator saturates after a few alternating training steps, the generator's gradients vanish and it can no longer learn.
The solution is to change the generator’s loss.
The original GANs paper appeared in 2014.
Early GAN results showed that generated samples were new, not mere memorizations of training data.
Early GANs worked wonderfully on MNIST.
Early GANs performed much worse on small black-and-white faces and were poor on more diverse datasets.
Initially, GANs were not yet competitive with other generative models.
DCGAN introduced a convolutional architecture for both generator and discriminator.
DCGAN started producing reasonable images on some datasets, though still small and flawed.
DCGAN was state of the art a decade ago.
Old generative modeling papers on GANs, VAEs, and the like often feature many bedroom images.
The Large Scale Scene Understanding (SU) dataset contains subsets of photos of different environments, including bedrooms.
The bedroom subset of the LSUN dataset became a standard benchmark after someone chose bedroom images for tests.
The bedroom pictures are small color images (64×64 or 128×128 pixels) designed to resemble real photographs.
A DCGAN after one epoch produces very bad images.
After five epochs, a DCGAN produces more or less okay images.
The five-epoch DCGAN results were acceptable at the time but are not exciting by today's standards.
It is important to understand whether a generative model is good.
The discriminator cannot reliably assess generative model quality.
A discriminator's failure to distinguish does not indicate that the generator produces good images or has a good latent space.
The discriminator's failure could be because it is undertrained or has limited capacity.
Visual inspection of generated images is used to evaluate whether the generator produces sensible results.
In a GAN, the generator maps a random noise vector $Z$ from the latent space to a point $X$ in pixel space.
Realistic images form an extremely complicated manifold in pixel space, and the latent space is meant to flatten that structure.
Our goal is to sample $Z$ from a simple distribution (e.g., a standard Gaussian) and have $G(Z)$ land on that manifold.
A popular test for a generator is a linear walk in the latent space.
When walking along the straight line from $Z_1$ to $Z_2$ in the latent space, all intermediate $Z$ should yield reasonable images.
If the generator $G$ simply memorized a few training points and mapped $Z$s to those, interpolated images would be nonsensical even if training images looked good.
A linear interpolation in pixel space would blend the two images by transparency rather than produce realistic intermediate photographs.
Ideally, the path in pixel space follows the manifold so that every step remains a realistic image.
Consistently observing that the interpolated images are realistic suggests the generator can produce realistic images from random $Z$.
In generative model papers, latent space walks are often shown with real or guaranteed good images at the ends and generated intermediates from interpolated $Z$.
The intermediate images may contain some artifacts but generally remain realistic.
Latent space walk interpolation results were state-of-the-art for image generation about ten years ago.
The rate of progress in image generation from ten years ago to now is remarkable.
The generated bedroom photos were not photorealistic; common failure modes included counting problems.
The recent meme about six fingers on a hand was still an issue a couple of years ago, but ten years ago it was much worse, e.g., three-headed dogs with many eyes.
Such failures make sense given the reverse convolutional architecture: it captures general features and then specializes local parts more or less independently, with limited context.
When generating an eye, the network may not know whether it is a left or right eye, so it might draw another eye, misaligning perspective.
These mistakes stand out to us because human vision is highly trained, but learning proper 3D perspective and object coherence is very difficult.
Among example images, it often takes a few questions for people to notice that one cat is actually a real photograph—just a sleeping, curled-up cat.
Distinguishing real from generated images is difficult.
By 2018, image generation had improved so much that imperfections are not visible to humans.
There are imperfections in generated faces, but on a slide they are not visible.
Comparing images from 2014 and 2017 shows tremendous progress in GAN-based generation in only a few years.
An important technical idea is that you do not need to generate a whole picture at once.
This can be cast as a conditional generation problem: you give a condition and the output changes accordingly.
A relatively simple version is super-resolution.

Super-resolution is a generative problem because you are inventing new detail when scaling a low-resolution image to high resolution, but it is easier than generating from scratch since the overall structure is given.
The idea for general generation was to start small and then apply a sequence of super-resolution steps.
This approach is called ProGAN, Progressive Growing GAN, which produced the famous realistic faces shown on the website ThisPersonDoesNotExist.
ProGAN first trains a simple GAN to generate 4×4 human faces; even from scratch this is not hard.
Then these 4×4 outputs are used as conditions for super-resolution to 8×8, then 16×16, 32×32, and so on.
Training took about two weeks on NVIDIA hardware, which provided a large compute advantage at the time, resulting in a 1-megapixel image of very high quality.
At the time of ProGAN, two main loss functions for GANs existed.
One was the least squares GAN, which addresses the saturation problem in a straightforward way.
Instead of using a sigmoid, it uses a squared deviation from a target constant (e.g., 1).
Overshooting the target is also penalized, so nothing blows up and everything clusters around the constant.
Least squares is usually a bad idea for classification, but here it works precisely because it avoids saturating gradients.
The conceptually deeper idea is the Wasserstein GAN (WGAN).
In machine learning, KL divergence is commonly used to measure closeness of distributions.
KL divergence is typically applied in relatively low-dimensional spaces.
In generative image models, $x$ is a very high-dimensional vector of pixel values.
The true data distribution $p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)$ and the generator distribution $p_g(x)$ are both concentrated in low-dimensional manifolds of that high-dimensional space.
Because each distribution lives on a thin subset, their supports are disjoint with probability one: where $p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)$ is non-zero, $p_g(x)$ is zero, and vice versa.
In this situation the KL divergence becomes infinite and meaningless.
Tweaking the generator a little bit—moving its line—does not change the infinite value, so the KL divergence provides no useful gradient for training.
Wasserstein distance was designed to solve exactly this problem of disjoint supports.
KL divergence provides no directional information for updating the generator when supports are disjoint.
The problem of disjoint supports seems to challenge much of machine learning, since distribution matching often involves separate subspaces.
In linear regression, the data and the modeled line do not overlap except at a single point of measure zero.
Yet the effect does not happen because we add noise.
Adding noise gives the assumed line a non-zero likelihood.
pData is fixed, but we smooth out pG by adding, for example, Gaussian noise, so $p_g(x) > 0$ everywhere.
It can be exponentially small, but that is enough.
We cannot match two distributions with disjoint or almost disjoint supports without modification.
In classical machine learning we add noise, so $p_g$ becomes a low‑dimensional model plus Gaussian noise extending over the whole space; then KL divergence works and we can maximize likelihood.
In linear regression we assume Gaussian noise around the line, learn the line, but when we predict a new point we do not add artificial noise—we simply use the expectation.
For implicit density generative models, we cannot drop the noise after training because the output already includes it.
Adding noise makes images blurry and unrealistic, so we do not want noise in such models.
The Wasserstein GAN therefore introduces a loss function that works without adding noise, based on the Earth Mover distance.
The Earth Mover (Wasserstein) distance can be understood by thinking of each distribution as a pile of earth with total volume 1.
Transporting earth requires work equal to mass times distance moved.
The Earth Mover distance is the minimal total work required to transform one distribution into the other under an optimal transport plan.
The goal is to match the two distributions while spending as little effort as possible.
In WGAN, the Earth Mover distance between real and generated distributions is minimized.
Minimizing Earth Mover distance involves a nested minimization, but mathematical techniques allow us to circumvent it.
The WGAN loss works even when the real and generated distributions have disjoint support—moving the generated distribution closer reduces the distance, so no artificial noise is needed.
Wasserstein GAN remains one of the most popular loss functions for GANs and adversarial training.
BigGAN, introduced in 2019, already produced reasonable images with nice interpolations.
For example, one can transition from a bird to a dog, and the intermediate artificial hybrids still kind of make sense.
The final idea, which leads into variational autoencoders and deepens our understanding of generative models, is the adversarial autoencoder.
The main challenge in generative modeling is defining a loss function: how do you measure whether a generated image is a good cat picture?
One natural answer is to train an autoencoder.
The autoencoder takes an image $X$ from pixel space, encodes it to a latent code $Z$ in a smaller, more understandable space, and then decodes $Z$ back to a reconstruction $\hat{X}$.
The autoencoder provides a straightforward $L_2$ loss between $X$ and $\hat{X}$, encouraging $Z$ to be a good compressed representation.
At first glance, the decoder looks like a generative model.
However, we cannot simply discard the encoder and use the decoder as a generative model.
The $X$'s live in a million-dimensional space, and even the relatively low-dimensional latent space (say 500 dimensions) contains a complicated manifold of $Z$'s from real images.
If we sample $Z$ from a standard Gaussian, we will almost never land on that manifold, and the decoded image will be nonsensical, not a nice cat picture.
To fix this and use autoencoders as generative models, we must regularize the latent space.
One approach is the variational autoencoder, to be discussed later.
An adversarial approach treats the $Z$'s coming from real images as fake, and lets the “real” $Z$'s be drawn from a simple prior such as a standard Gaussian.
A discriminator is placed not on images but on latent codes, to distinguish between the encoded latent codes and samples from the prior.
The encoder is trained to fool the discriminator.
If the discriminator cannot tell them apart, then sampling $Z$ from the standard Gaussian should yield latent codes that the decoder interprets as realistic images.
The adversarial autoencoder is an old idea, nearly as old as GANs themselves.
Variational autoencoders offer a cleaner conceptual solution and are more widely used, but adversarial autoencoders can sometimes perform better depending on the implementation.
Adversarial autoencoders can be modified straightforwardly; for example, to generate a specific MNIST digit you can condition the distributions on labels.
GANs were state-of-the-art for image generation around 2020 and remain important in specific domains such as super-resolution and style transfer (via StyleGAN models).
For straightforward image generation or text-to-image tasks, GANs have been completely replaced by diffusion models.

summary.text: The term “generative AI” is broad.
Logistic regression defines a probability distribution over classes.
In this context, the focus is on models that produce high-dimensional, structured objects (images, text, music).
Among neural-network-based deep generative models, the primary fork is between explicit density models and implicit density models.
Explicit density models provide or approximate a formula for $p(x)$, the probability of observing a data point $x$.
Explicit density models split into tractable density and approximate density.
Tractable density models are those where the density $p(x)$ can be written down directly.
Autoregressive models use the chain rule $p(x)=p(x_1)p(x_2|x_1)\dots p(x_n|x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})$ and parametrise the conditionals, e.g., with an RNN or Transformer.
Most large language models are autoregressive.
For images, PixelCNN generated pixels sequentially but was too slow for high resolution.
Flow-based models compose many simple invertible transformations: $x = f_k \circ \dots \circ f_1(z)$, so that a simple $z$ distribution is transformed into a complex one.
Approximate density models approximate $p(x)$ by a simpler distribution $q$.
The main example of an approximate density model is the Variational Autoencoder (VAE).
VAE uses a variational bound to derive a tractable loss.
Diffusion models often operate in a VAE’s latent space.
Implicit density models do not supply a formula for $p(x)$; they are pure samplers.
The most prominent member of implicit density models is the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN).

In a GAN, a noise vector $Z$ sampled from a simple distribution (e.g., a standard Gaussian) is mapped through a neural network to produce a sample $\hat{X}$ that should be indistinguishable from real data.
The distribution of $\hat{X}$ is implicit—there is no access to its density.
The central challenge of generative modelling is defining the loss function (e.g., “what makes a good cat picture?”).
There is no closed-form answer to this challenge.
GANs address this challenge by learning the loss itself.
A GAN consists of two networks: a generator and a discriminator.
The generator $G = G(z;\theta_g): Z \to X$ takes random noise $z \sim p_z$ and produces a sample $\hat{x} = G(z)$.
The discriminator $D = D(x;\theta_d): X \to [0,1]$ is a binary classifier that outputs the probability that $x$ is real (1) rather than generated (0).
The discriminator sees real samples $x \sim p_{\text{data}}$ and fake samples $\hat{x} \sim p_g$, where $p_g$ is the distribution induced by $G$.
The discriminator is trained to maximize the probability of assigning the correct label.
The generator is trained to fool the discriminator, i.e., to make $D(G(z))$ large.
Early in training the generator is poor and the discriminator untrained.
Training alternates: improve $D$ slightly, then improve $G$ to catch up.
Ideally, training repeats until $p_g = p_{\text{data}}$ and the discriminator cannot do better than random guessing.
In practice, this ideal is seldom reached.
The discriminator solves a binary classification problem with the objective: $\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{data}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g(x)}[\log(1 - D(x))]$.
$p_g(x) = G_{\#}p_z$ is the pushforward of the noise distribution.
Real samples are assigned label 1, generated samples label 0.
The generator originally minimized $\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]$.

Together with the discriminator's objective, this gives the minimax game $\min_G \max_D V(D,G)$, where $V(D,G) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{data}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]$.
For a fixed generator $G$, the optimal discriminator is given by $D^*_G(x) = \frac{p_\text{data}(x)}{p_\text{data}(x) + p_g(x)}$.
Substituting $D^*_G$ into the generator's objective shows that the global minimum is attained if and only if $p_g = p_{\text{data}}$.
At the optimum, the criterion equals the Jensen–Shannon divergence between $p_{\text{data}}$ and $p_g$.

The Jensen–Shannon divergence is defined as $\operatorname{JS}(p_\text{data} \| p_g) = \frac12\operatorname{KL}\!\left(p_\text{data} \bigg\| \frac{p_\text{data}+p_g}{2}\right) + \frac12\operatorname{KL}\!\left(p_g \bigg\| \frac{p_\text{data}+p_g}{2}\right)$.
These theoretical results are largely irrelevant in practice.
The generator never uses the original loss in practice.
The reason is the saturating gradient problem.
Minimizing $\mathbb{E}_{z}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]$ uses a sigmoid at the discriminator’s output.
When the discriminator is confident and correct, its gradient saturates because $D(G(z)) \approx 0$ leads to $\log(1 - D(G(z))) \approx 0$.
The generator then receives a vanishing learning signal and can no longer improve.
The solution is to flip the loss: maximize the probability of the discriminator being wrong.
The practical generator loss is $-\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log D(G(z))]$.
With this loss, when the discriminator is confident, the loss is large and gradients flow; as the generator improves, the gradients diminish naturally.
This flipped loss is used in all practical GAN training.
Training alternates between two steps.
Step 1: Fix $G$ and update $D$ to maximize $\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{data}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g(x)}[\log(1 - D(x))]$.
Step 2: Fix $D$ and update $G$ to minimize $-\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log D(G(z))]$ (which is equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood of the discriminator being wrong).
Early GANs (Goodfellow et al., 2014) generated new samples, not memorizations.
Early GANs worked well on MNIST but poorly on more diverse images.
The original GANs produced only tiny, low-quality images.
DCGAN (Radford et al., 2016) introduced key architectural stabilizers.
DCGAN used strided convolutions instead of pooling layers.
DCGAN used batch normalization in both generator and discriminator.
DCGAN removed fully connected layers.
DCGAN used the Adam optimizer.
On LSUN bedrooms at 64×64 resolution, after one epoch of DCGAN training, only coarse room structures appear.
After five epochs, the images become much sharper and more realistic.
A discriminator that merely fails to distinguish real from fake does not guarantee that the generator understands the data manifold, because the discriminator might be undertrained.
A more convincing test is a linear walk in latent space.
In a linear walk, two latent vectors $z_1, z_2$ are interpolated: $z(\alpha) = (1-\alpha)z_1 + \alpha z_2$.
If the generator has learned a smooth manifold, every interpolated $z$ should decode to a plausible image.
If the generator memorized training points, interpolated images will be nonsensical blurs.
This walk is often displayed in papers with the two endpoints as real images and the intermediate frames generated.
The linear walk shows that the latent space captures meaningful structure.
In DCGAN, removing filters that detect windows removes windows from generated images.
In DCGAN, vector arithmetic in latent space works: “man with glasses” – “man” + “woman” yields “woman with glasses”.
DCGAN was applied to pixel art from NES games.
DCGAN struggles with counting objects (e.g., too many eyes, limbs).
DCGAN struggles with perspective.
The reason is that convolutional generators assemble local features with limited global context.
A major breakthrough came with ProGAN (Karras et al., 2017) from NVIDIA.
The key idea of ProGAN is to avoid generating a full-resolution image from scratch.
ProGAN first trains a GAN to produce small images (e.g., 4×4), then stacks super-resolution steps, each doubling the resolution, up to 1024×1024.
Because each stage works on a relatively easy sub-problem, the whole training is more stable and faster.
More data can be shown in the same wall-clock time.
In ProGAN, new layers are added progressively.
The discriminator in ProGAN remains roughly symmetric to the generator.
For some categories, resolution in ProGAN is stopped at 256×256, which already looks excellent.
ProGAN training took about two weeks on large NVIDIA hardware at the time.
ProGAN yielded famous photorealistic faces seen on websites like *This Person Does Not Exist*.
The ProGAN authors compared Least Squares GAN and Wasserstein GAN losses.
This comparison motivated the deeper study of loss functions.
The original GAN loss suffered from vanishing gradients when the discriminator became too confident.
LSGAN (Mao et al., 2016) addresses this by replacing the sigmoid cross-entropy with a quadratic loss.
LSGAN discriminator loss: $\min_D \frac12 \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_\text{data}}[(D(x) - b)^2] + \frac12 \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[(D(G(z)) - a)^2]$.
LSGAN generator loss: $\min_G \frac12 \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[(D(G(z)) - c)^2]$.
The discriminator learns to output $a$ for fake samples and $b$ for real samples.
The generator wants the discriminator to output $c$ on fake samples.
Typically $a=0$, $b=c=1$.
Because overshooting the target is also penalized, the LSGAN loss avoids saturation.
LSGAN provides smooth gradients even when the discriminator is very accurate.
LSGAN is more robust to architectural choices.
LSGAN suffers less from mode collapse.
In a standard GAN, the input is a monolithic noise vector $z$.
InfoGAN (Chen et al., 2016) splits the input into two parts: $z$ and $c$.
$z$ is incompressible noise, the source of randomness.
$c = c_1 c_2 \dots c_L$ is a latent code whose dimensions correspond to interpretable factors of variation.
The generator becomes $G(z,c)$.
Without extra pressure, $G$ could ignore $c$.
InfoGAN maximizes the mutual information $I(c, G(z,c))$.
It uses a variational lower bound parameterized by a neural network $Q$, which often shares most of $D$.
On MNIST, using $c = (c_1, c_2, c_3)$, $c_1$ is a discrete 10-way code with uniform prior that learns digits without supervised labels.
$c_2$ and $c_3$ are continuous codes uniformly sampled from $[-1,1]$ that control properties like slant and thickness.
A classifier trained only on $c_1$ achieves 5% error on MNIST with zero labels.
InfoGAN also works on 3D faces and chairs.
Wasserstein GAN (Arjovsky et al., 2017) tackles why KL divergence and JS divergence fail in high-dimensional generative modeling.
In image generation, both $p_{\text{data}}$ and $p_g$ are concentrated on low-dimensional manifolds in high-dimensional pixel space.
Their supports are almost disjoint.
Where $p_{\text{data}}(x) > 0$, $p_g(x) \approx 0$, and vice versa.
The KL divergence then becomes infinite and provides no useful gradient.
Small changes to the generator keep the KL divergence infinite, so it cannot guide learning.
In classical problems like linear regression, adding Gaussian noise spreads $p_g$ over the full space, making KL divergence well-defined.
For image generation, adding noise makes the output blurry and unrealistic; crisp samples are desired without artificial noise.
The Earth Mover (Wasserstein-1) distance is designed for situations where distributions have disjoint supports.
The Wasserstein distance is the minimal physical work (mass × distance) to transform one distribution into the other.
It varies smoothly even when supports do not overlap.

The Wasserstein distance is defined as $W(p_{\text{data}}, p_{\text{model}}) = \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(p_{\text{data}}, p_{\text{model}})} \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim \gamma}[\|x - y\|]$, where $\Pi$ is the set of joint distributions with the given marginals.
Example: For $Z \sim U[0,1]$, $\mathbb{P}_0$ as distribution of $(0,Z)$, and $g_\theta(z) = (\theta, z)$, as $\theta \to 0$, only the EM distance converges continuously, while JS and KL diverge.

The Kantorovich–Rubinstein dual form is $W(p_{\text{data}}, p_{\text{model}}) = \sup_{\|f\|_L \le 1} ( \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{model}}}[f(x)] )$, over 1-Lipschitz functions.
In WGAN, the discriminator is replaced with a critic $f_w$ whose output is a real number, not a probability.
For a fixed generator, the critic is trained to maximize $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\text{data}}}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_z}[f(g_\theta(z))]$.
The generator gradient is $\nabla_\theta W = -\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[\nabla_\theta f_w(g_\theta(z))]$.
To enforce the 1-Lipschitz constraint, weight clipping can be used: clamp the weights of $f_w$ to a small interval after each update.
In WGAN, the critic can be trained to convergence, unlike the discriminator in an ordinary GAN.
The WGAN loss value strongly correlates with sample quality, serving as a reliable metric.
WGAN is far more robust to architectural choices.
WGAN works even without batch normalization or with fewer filters.
Improved WGAN (WGAN-GP) replaces weight clipping with a gradient penalty.
Weight clipping can cause exploding/vanishing gradients and limit the critic’s capacity.
The gradient penalty is $\lambda \,\mathbb{E}_{\hat{x} \sim \mathbb{P}_{\hat{x}}}[(\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1)^2]$.
$\hat{x}$ is sampled uniformly along straight lines between real and generated examples.
This softer regularization is now standard.
Convolutional generators have a strictly local receptive field.
Convolutional generators make it hard to capture long-range dependencies.
An example of a long-range dependency is ensuring a dog has exactly one tail, in the right place.
Self‑Attention GAN (Zhang et al., 2019) adapts the self‑attention mechanism from Transformers to images.
In Self‑Attention GAN, the generator can attend to distant regions while drawing.
Visualisations of the attention maps of Self‑Attention GAN confirm that the generator attends to distant regions when needed.
BigGAN (Brock et al., 2019) combined SAGAN with extra architectural tricks and massive compute.
BigGAN pushed the Inception score threefold.
BigGAN produced high‑quality, diverse images with smooth interpolations.
Transitioning from a bird to a dog with BigGAN yields plausible intermediate artificial animals.
Assessing the quality of generated images is hard.
The Inception Score (Salimans et al., 2016) provides an automatic metric for assessing the quality of generated images.
The Inception Score involves passing each generated image $x$ through a pre-trained Inception classifier to obtain the conditional label distribution $p(y \mid x)$.
A good generator should produce images that are unambiguous, meaning the conditional label distribution $p(y \mid x)$ has low entropy.
A good generator should produce diverse images, meaning the marginal distribution $p(y)=\int p(y \mid G(z))\,dz$ has high entropy.
The Inception Score is computed as $\exp\!\big(\mathbb{E}_x \operatorname{KL}(p(y \mid x) \| p(y))\big)$.
The Inception Score cannot be used directly as a training loss.
The Inception Score is a widely used evaluation metric.
A plain autoencoder trained with an $L_2$ reconstruction loss does not yield a usable generative model.
The latent vectors $Z$ coming from real images form a complicated manifold inside the latent space.
A $Z$ sampled from a simple prior, such as a standard Gaussian, almost never lies on the manifold of real image latent vectors.
If a $Z$ sampled from a simple prior does not lie on the manifold, the decoder will produce garbage, not a realistic image.
Adversarial Autoencoders (Makhzani et al., 2015) place a discriminator on the latent codes $Z$.
In Adversarial Autoencoders, the discriminator tries to distinguish between encoded vectors $E(x)$ as fake and samples from a chosen prior as real.
In Adversarial Autoencoders, the encoder is trained to reconstruct well and to fool the latent discriminator.
In Adversarial Autoencoders, when the distribution of encoded vectors matches the prior distribution, sampling $Z$ from the prior and decoding yields realistic outputs.
Adversarial Autoencoders are conceptually almost as old as GANs.
Variational autoencoders provide a cleaner variational solution compared to Adversarial Autoencoders.
Adversarial Autoencoders still find use in practice.
Adversarial Autoencoders have been applied to molecule generation in oncology (Kadurin et al., 2017, 2018).
Adversarial Autoencoders have been used in the MOSES benchmark for generative chemistry (Polikovsky et al., 2018).
In a Conditional GAN (Mirza and Osindero, 2014), both generator and discriminator receive an additional conditioning vector $y$.
The generator in a Conditional GAN is defined as $G = G(z, y; \theta_g)$.
The discriminator in a Conditional GAN is defined as $D = D(x, y; \theta_d)$.
Conditional GANs allow controlled generation.
Conditional GANs have been applied to face aging (Antipov et al., 2017).
Conditional GANs have been applied to super-resolution with ESRGAN (Ledig et al., 2017).
Stacked Generative Adversarial Networks (Huang et al., 2017) chain multiple GANs sequentially.
In Stacked GANs, each generator $G_i$ learns lower-level representations by roughly inverting a deep encoder $E_i$.
In Stacked GANs, the generator $G_i$ is conditioned on the next-stage representation $h_{i+1}$.
In Stacked GANs, the output of $G_i$ is forced to reconstruct $h_{i+1}$ via the encoder $E_i$.
In Stacked GANs, the conditional loss is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{cond}} = \mathbb{E}_{h_{i+1}\sim p_{\text{data}},\, z_i\sim p_{z_i}}\!\big[d\big(E_i(G_i(h_{i+1}, z_i)),\, h_{i+1}\big)\big]$.
In Stacked GANs, the entropy loss is used to prevent the generator $G_i$ from ignoring the noise $z_i$.

In Stacked GANs, the entropy loss is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{ent}} = \mathbb{E}_{z_i \sim p_{z_i}}\!\Big[ \mathbb{E}_{\hat{h}_i \sim G_i(\hat{h}_i \mid z_i)} \big[-\log Q_i(z_i \mid \hat{h}_i)\big] \Big]$.
In the entropy loss, $Q_i$ is a neural approximation to the posterior $p_i(z_i \mid \hat{h}_i)$.
Stacked GANs outperformed earlier models.
Progressive Growing (ProGAN) remains stronger than Stacked GANs for image synthesis.
GANs were the state-of-the-art for image generation around 2020.
GANs remain important for super-resolution, style transfer (StyleGAN), and other conditional tasks.
For general text-to-image generation, GANs have been superseded by diffusion models.
Diffusion models will be covered in the final lecture.
